explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary biliary cirrhosis results from prolonged extrahepatic biliary obstruction, in which sustained cholestasis and back-pressure drive progressive hepatic fibrosis and eventual cirrhosis, emphasizing the importance of relieving obstruction promptly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gallstone ileus arises from a stone eroding into the bowel, not from chronic ductal obstruction and cholestasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Porcelain gallbladder results from chronic cholecystitis with mural calcification, not from a distal duct stricture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute pancreatitis follows an obstructing stone at the ampulla, an acute event rather than the chronic fibrotic outcome described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pigment stone formation is driven by hemolysis and increased bilirubin load, not by prolonged mechanical obstruction causing cirrhosis.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman undergoes abdominal CT for unrelated flank pain. An incidental 3-cm right-lobe liver lesion is noted. On contrast imaging it shows discontinuous peripheral nodular enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal fill-in on delayed phases. Liver function tests are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in is the classic imaging signature of a hepatic hemangioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemangiomas are cavernous vascular channels with slow blood flow, producing the characteristic edge (peripheral nodular) enhancement that progressively fills toward the center on delayed images. They are the most common benign liver tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FNH typically shows homogeneous arterial enhancement with a central stellate scar, not peripheral nodular fill-in.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCC classically shows arterial hyperenhancement with washout in the portal/delayed phase, not centripetal fill-in, and usually arises in cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenoma is a hypervascular lesion that enhances briskly and homogeneously in the arterial phase, without the peripheral discontinuous pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cholangiocarcinoma tends to show delayed, progressive enhancement of fibrous stroma but not the peripheral nodular pattern of a vascular lesion.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with no significant medical history has a well-circumscribed 4-cm liver mass discovered incidentally. Contrast-enhanced MRI shows homogeneous arterial enhancement and a central stellate scar. She takes no medications and denies alcohol or trauma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A central stellate scar with homogeneous arterial enhancement is characteristic of focal nodular hyperplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: FNH is the second most common benign liver mass, composed of hyperplastic hepatocytes arranged around a central fibrous scar. The central stellate scar is the key testable imaging feature distinguishing it from other lesions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenoma is strongly linked to oral contraceptive use (which she denies) and does not have a central scar; it carries hemorrhage and malignancy risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in, not a central scar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCC arises in cirrhosis, shows arterial enhancement with washout, and does not feature a benign central stellate scar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastases are typically multiple and do not display a central stellate scar.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who has taken combined oral contraceptives for 6 years is found to have a solitary, well-demarcated 5-cm mass in the right hepatic lobe. Imaging shows a hypervascular lesion with brisk homogeneous arterial enhancement and no central scar. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A young woman on oral contraceptives with a solitary hypervascular right-lobe mass lacking a central scar is classic for hepatic adenoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocytes contain estrogen receptors, so adenomas grow with oral contraceptive and androgen use. They are usually solitary right-lobe lesions in women aged 20-44 and lack the central scar of FNH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FNH characteristically has a central stellate scar and is not strongly hormone-dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in, a different vascular pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholangiocarcinoma is a biliary adenocarcinoma of older patients with obstructive jaundice, not a hypervascular mass in a young woman.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatoblastoma is a malignant tumor of young children, not adults.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C and established cirrhosis presents with new-onset ascites, jaundice, and weight loss. CT shows a solitary 6-cm hepatic mass with arterial enhancement and portal-venous washout. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Cirrhosis with a solitary enhancing/washout mass and elevated AFP is diagnostic of hepatocellular carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCC is the most common primary liver cancer and usually arises in cirrhosis from hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or alcohol. The combination of a characteristic mass on imaging plus elevated AFP establishes the diagnosis without biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemangioma is a benign vascular lesion with centripetal fill-in and does not raise AFP or cause decompensation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FNH is a benign lesion with a central scar and no AFP elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholangiocarcinoma is a biliary adenocarcinoma associated with CA 19-9 and obstructive jaundice, not AFP elevation in cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenoma occurs in young women on oral contraceptives and does not elevate AFP.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of resected colon adenocarcinoma is found on surveillance CT to have multiple bilobar liver lesions of varying sizes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these hepatic lesions?

explanation.summary: Multiple bilobar liver lesions in a patient with a known primary cancer represent metastases, the most common malignant liver lesions overall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metastasis (from sites such as colon, breast, and lung) is the most common cause of a cancerous lesion in the liver overall and characteristically produces multiple lesions, in contrast to a solitary primary tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCC typically presents as a solitary mass in a cirrhotic liver, not multiple lesions in a patient with colon cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiosarcoma is a rare primary tumor tied to arsenic/vinyl chloride exposure, not the typical explanation for multiple lesions after colon cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FNH is a single benign lesion, not a multifocal malignant process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from the biliary tree and does not typically explain multiple metastatic-appearing deposits following a colon primary.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents with painless jaundice, pruritus, and a palpable gallbladder. MRCP demonstrates a stricturing mass at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts with intrahepatic biliary dilation. Which of the following best describes this tumor?

explanation.summary: A cholangiocarcinoma at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts is a Klatskin (hilar) tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Klatskin tumors arise at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts and are the most common cholangiocarcinoma subtype (60%-70% of cases), presenting with obstructive jaundice and intrahepatic ductal dilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distal cholangiocarcinoma involves the common bile duct near the pancreas, not the hepatic duct confluence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises within the liver parenchyma peripheral to the hilum and comprises only about 5%-10% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gallbladder carcinoma originates in the gallbladder wall and is excluded from the term cholangiocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ampullary carcinoma arises at the ampulla of Vater and is likewise excluded from cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a biopsy-proven hepatic adenoma has a lesion that has grown to 6 cm and now causes intermittent right upper quadrant pain. She currently takes combined oral contraceptives. In addition to discontinuing the oral contraceptives, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Routine observation with annual ultrasound only

explanation.summary: A symptomatic hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm should be surgically resected because of hemorrhage and malignant transformation risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adenomas carry a risk of spontaneous hemorrhage and low-rate malignant transformation to HCC. Management includes stopping estrogen/androgen exposure and resecting lesions that are symptomatic or greater than 5 cm, as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Observation alone is inadequate for a symptomatic adenoma greater than 5 cm because of bleeding and malignancy risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemotherapy has no role in a benign hepatic adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radioembolization is not standard therapy for a resectable symptomatic adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplantation is reserved for rare cases such as adenomatosis or unresectable disease, not a single resectable 6-cm lesion.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A hepatologist is teaching about the leading causes of hepatocellular carcinoma using the 'ABC' mnemonic. Which of the following sets correctly represents the three most common causes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus

explanation.summary: The 'ABC' causes of HCC are Alcohol, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCC most often develops in cirrhosis, and chronic hepatitis B/C plus alcohol account for the great majority of cases; HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis alone accounts for about 75% of HCC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aflatoxin is a risk factor and biliary cysts/Clonorchis relate to cholangiocarcinoma, but this set is not the ABC mnemonic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenoma, bile stasis, and cirrhosis are not the three leading HCC causes captured by ABC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoimmune hepatitis, biopsy, and chemotherapy do not constitute the ABC causes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arsenic and vinyl chloride relate to hepatic angiosarcoma, not the ABC causes of HCC.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a 4-cm liver mass with classic arterial enhancement and venous washout on triple-phase CT, and his alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. A trainee suggests obtaining a percutaneous biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before treatment. Why is biopsy generally avoided in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It requires general anesthesia that cirrhotic patients cannot tolerate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is unable to detect malignant hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: It risks hemorrhage and seeding of tumor cells along the needle tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: It delays diagnosis by several weeks awaiting pathology

explanation.summary: Biopsy is avoided in suspected HCC because of hemorrhage risk and needle-tract/peritoneal tumor seeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCC is highly vascular, so biopsy risks significant bleeding, and it can seed malignant cells along the tract or into the peritoneum. When imaging is characteristic and AFP is elevated, the diagnosis can be made without biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Percutaneous liver biopsy does not require general anesthesia; anesthesia risk is not the reason it is avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Biopsy can detect malignant hepatocytes; poor detection is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biopsy does not alter AFP levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The concern is bleeding and seeding, not a diagnostic delay from processing time.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and known primary sclerosing cholangitis develops progressive painless jaundice, weight loss, and pruritus over 2 months. Laboratory studies show a cholestatic pattern and elevated CA 19-9. Which of the following malignancies is he at greatest risk for?

explanation.summary: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (often with ulcerative colitis) is a major risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic biliary inflammation and cholestasis in PSC promote malignant transformation of cholangiocytes. Painless obstructive jaundice with elevated CA 19-9 in a PSC patient strongly suggests cholangiocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCC arises from hepatocytes in cirrhosis and is associated with AFP, not the biliary/CA 19-9 picture of PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemangioma is a benign vascular lesion, not a malignancy linked to PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiosarcoma relates to arsenic and vinyl chloride exposure, not PSC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatoblastoma is a pediatric tumor, unrelated to PSC in an adult.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 48-year-old asymptomatic man is found to have a 2.5-cm hepatic hemangioma on ultrasound performed for gallstones. He has no abdominal symptoms and normal liver function tests. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic hepatic hemangiomas require no treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemangiomas are benign vascular lesions with no malignant potential. Asymptomatic lesions need no intervention; treatment is reserved for persistent symptoms or complications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resection is reserved for large symptomatic or complicated hemangiomas, not an asymptomatic 2.5-cm lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Embolization is not indicated for a small asymptomatic hemangioma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chemotherapy has no role in a benign vascular lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biopsy is generally avoided in hemangiomas because of bleeding risk and is unnecessary when imaging is diagnostic.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who worked for decades in a polyvinyl chloride manufacturing plant develops a rapidly enlarging, multifocal hemorrhagic liver malignancy of endothelial origin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A vinyl chloride/arsenic-associated malignant endothelial liver tumor is a hepatic angiosarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a rare primary liver malignancy of endothelial origin classically associated with arsenic, vinyl chloride, and Thorotrast exposure, often presenting as a hemorrhagic multifocal tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCC is a hepatocyte-derived tumor of cirrhosis, not an endothelial malignancy linked to vinyl chloride.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholangiocarcinoma is a biliary epithelial adenocarcinoma, not of endothelial origin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FNH is a benign hyperplastic lesion, not a malignant endothelial tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenoma is a benign hepatocellular tumor associated with oral contraceptives, not vinyl chloride.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 24-year-old competitive bodybuilder who has used anabolic-androgenic steroids for several years is found to have a solitary vascular liver lesion that ruptures, causing intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Which of the following benign tumors is most strongly associated with his steroid use?

explanation.summary: Anabolic androgenic steroid use is strongly associated with hepatic adenoma, which is prone to hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocytes carry hormone receptors, so both estrogens (oral contraceptives) and androgens (anabolic steroids) drive hepatic adenoma formation. Adenomas are highly vascular and can rupture and bleed, as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FNH is not strongly hormone-dependent and has essentially no risk of hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemangiomas are common but are not specifically driven by anabolic steroids and rarely rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bile duct hamartomas are small incidental benign lesions unrelated to steroids and do not bleed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Simple hepatic cysts are fluid-filled and unrelated to androgen use.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a 3-cm liver lesion confidently diagnosed as focal nodular hyperplasia based on characteristic MRI findings including a central stellate scar. She is asymptomatic. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has a high risk of malignant transformation and should be resected

choices.label: B
choices.text: It frequently ruptures and causes life-threatening hemorrhage

choices.label: C
choices.text: It requires lifelong every-3-month imaging surveillance

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has no meaningful risk of hemorrhage or malignancy and needs no treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: It should be treated with liver transplantation

explanation.summary: FNH is benign with no meaningful risk of hemorrhage or malignant transformation and requires no treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: FNH is composed of hyperplastic hepatocytes around a central scar and contains normal bile ducts and portal structures. It is not strongly hormone-dependent and carries no meaningful risk of bleeding or malignancy, so no treatment or routine follow-up is needed once confidently diagnosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FNH does not have a high malignant potential and does not require resection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Unlike adenoma, FNH does not frequently hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intensive lifelong surveillance is unnecessary for a confidently diagnosed FNH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplantation is not indicated for a benign FNH.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who immigrated from Southeast Asia and frequently ate raw freshwater fish presents with obstructive jaundice and an intrahepatic biliary mass. Chronic infection with which of the following organisms is the most likely predisposing risk factor?

explanation.summary: Clonorchis sinensis, the Chinese liver fluke acquired from raw freshwater fish, is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clonorchis sinensis is a parasitic flatworm common in Asia acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish; chronic biliary infection causes inflammation predisposing to cholangiocarcinoma, matching this patient's biliary tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis B predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma, not the biliary/fluke-related cholangiocarcinoma described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Echinococcus causes hydatid cysts, not cholangiocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic liver abscess, not biliary malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistosoma mansoni causes periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension but is not the classic fluke linked to cholangiocarcinoma (that is Clonorchis/Opisthorchis).

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with no history of liver disease, no cirrhosis, no viral hepatitis, and a normal alpha-fetoprotein is found to have a large solitary liver tumor. Resected pathology shows large polygonal eosinophilic malignant hepatocytes separated by dense lamellar fibrous bands. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A young patient without cirrhosis, normal AFP, and lamellar fibrous bands on histology has fibrolamellar HCC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrolamellar HCC occurs in young adults without underlying liver disease or cirrhosis, typically has a normal AFP, and is defined histologically by malignant hepatocytes surrounded by dense lamellar collagen bands. It carries a relatively better prognosis when resectable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conventional HCC arises in older cirrhotic patients and usually raises AFP, unlike this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholangiocarcinoma is a mucin-producing biliary adenocarcinoma, not a hepatocyte tumor with lamellar fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FNH is benign hyperplasia, not a malignant tumor with atypical hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial tumor, not composed of eosinophilic hepatocytes in fibrous bands.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a known large hepatocellular carcinoma is admitted with recurrent episodes of confusion and diaphoresis. Fingerstick glucose during episodes is 38 mg/dL, and he is also noted to have an elevated hematocrit. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paraneoplastic ectopic hormone/factor production by the tumor

explanation.summary: HCC can produce paraneoplastic syndromes, including hypoglycemia and erythrocytosis, via ectopic factor production.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCC is a classic cause of paraneoplastic syndromes: ectopic production of IGF-like factors can cause hypoglycemia, and erythropoietin-like activity causes erythrocytosis (elevated hematocrit). This explains both the low glucose and the polycythemia in a patient with a large HCC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion but does not produce hypoglycemia with erythrocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An insulinoma could cause hypoglycemia but would not explain erythrocytosis, and is not implied by a known HCC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycemia but not erythrocytosis, and is not the classic HCC association.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron overload does not produce this combination of hypoglycemia and erythrocytosis.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a long history of cholelithiasis undergoes ultrasound showing a calcified 'porcelain' gallbladder wall. She reports chronic right upper quadrant discomfort and weight loss. This finding most strongly raises concern for which of the following malignancies?

explanation.summary: A porcelain (calcified) gallbladder is a risk factor for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic inflammation from gallstones leading to a calcified porcelain gallbladder is associated with gallbladder carcinoma, most commonly adenocarcinoma. The chronic gallstone history and constitutional symptoms fit this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HCC arises from hepatocytes in cirrhosis, not from a calcified gallbladder wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises within the liver parenchyma, not the gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Angiosarcoma is a rare toxin-associated liver tumor, unrelated to porcelain gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ampullary carcinoma arises at the ampulla of Vater, not from the gallbladder wall.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with progressive abdominal distension. Examination reveals a firm right upper quadrant mass, and imaging shows a large solitary hepatic tumor. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A young child with a solitary liver mass and markedly elevated AFP most likely has hepatoblastoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor of young children (typically under age 3), presenting as a solitary hepatic mass with elevated alpha-fetoprotein, matching this toddler.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCC is a tumor of adults with chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, not the typical liver malignancy of a 2-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholangiocarcinoma is a biliary adenocarcinoma of older adults, not a pediatric mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FNH is a benign lesion of adults, mostly young women, and does not elevate AFP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infantile hemangioma is benign and does not markedly elevate AFP as a solid malignant mass would.

questions.topicName: Hepatic and Biliary Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis is diagnosed with a solitary 3-cm hepatocellular carcinoma confined to the liver, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Which of the following offers the best chance of cure?

explanation.summary: Localized HCC is best treated for cure with surgical resection or liver transplantation.
explanation.whyCorrect: For localized HCC, resection and liver transplantation are the most efficacious, potentially curative treatments (5-year survival 30%-50% after surgery). Transplantation is especially favorable in cirrhotic patients meeting criteria, as it treats both the tumor and underlying liver disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy is largely ineffective for HCC and is not curative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiation therapy is not a standard curative treatment for HCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Palliative care is inappropriate as first-line management for a curable localized tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Repeat biopsy provides no therapy and risks bleeding and tumor seeding.
